events.title: A Trip to the Moon Released
events.blurb: A former stage magician released a 14-minute narrative film depicting a group of astronomers launched to the Moon in a giant bullet fired from a cannon, encountering hostile selenites, and returning to Earth. Its hand-tinted prints included the most recognizable image in early cinema: a cartoon Moon with a bullet lodged in its eye. It was pirated within months by Thomas Edison's company, which sold copies without paying royalties.
events.revealBlurb: 1902 — Georges Méliès, whose production company Star Film went bankrupt partly from lost piracy revenue. He destroyed many of his own negatives in bitterness; the hand-coloured version was rediscovered in Barcelona in 1993, disintegrating, and painstakingly restored.

events.title: The Birth of a Nation Premieres
events.blurb: An American director released a three-hour silent film about a Southern family during the Civil War and Reconstruction, pioneering cinematic techniques that remain standard: close-ups, cross-cutting, battle-scene camera movement. The film portrayed the Ku Klux Klan as heroic and Black people (played mostly by white actors in blackface) as subhuman. Its release coincided with a revival of the real Klan, which had been inactive for 40 years.
events.revealBlurb: February 8, 1915 — D.W. Griffith at Clune's Auditorium, Los Angeles. President Woodrow Wilson hosted a White House screening, calling it "history written with lightning." The NAACP's protest against it was the organization's first major campaign.

events.title: First Academy Awards
events.blurb: A 15-minute banquet at a Hollywood hotel awarded twelve statuettes — a 34 cm tall gilded figure of a knight standing on a reel of film — to films, actors, directors, and technicians selected by the newly formed Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences. 270 people attended. The winners had been announced three months earlier. The whole ceremony received brief mention in the next day's Los Angeles Times, on page 10.
events.revealBlurb: May 16, 1929 — Hollywood Roosevelt Hotel. First Best Picture: "Wings." Best Actor: Emil Jannings. The bronze statuette's nickname, "Oscar," was supposedly coined by an Academy librarian who thought it resembled her Uncle Oscar; the story is almost certainly retrofitted.

events.title: Citizen Kane Released
events.blurb: A 25-year-old radio and theatre prodigy made his feature film directing debut with a quasi-biographical study of a newspaper tycoon, structurally organized as a series of flashback interviews about the man's last word ("Rosebud"). The film used deep-focus cinematography, low-angle setups, overlapping dialogue, and non-linear structure in ways that rewrote the cinematic grammar of the next 70 years. Its real-life subject, a media baron, tried to have every print destroyed.
events.revealBlurb: May 1, 1941 — Orson Welles, age 25. The target was William Randolph Hearst, who banned mention of the film in his newspapers. It lost Best Picture to "How Green Was My Valley." It tops nearly every "greatest films of all time" list.

events.title: Star Wars Released
events.blurb: A 33-year-old American director released a science-fiction film mashing up elements of samurai cinema, WWII dogfight pictures, and Joseph Campbell's monomyth theory, with groundbreaking effects assembled in a repurposed warehouse with a workforce assembled from scratch. The studio had cut his budget and expected the film to flop; one executive had retitled it "The Adventures of Luke Starkiller." Lines began forming at theatres on opening morning and did not stop for years.
events.revealBlurb: May 25, 1977 — George Lucas. He traded his directing salary for merchandising rights; he became a billionaire. The effects company he had to build from scratch, Industrial Light & Magic, became the industry standard for decades. Campbell wept watching the film.

events.title: Stockton-Darlington Railway Opens
events.blurb: A 40-kilometre railway built to carry coal from the inland pits of County Durham to the shipping harbour at Stockton-on-Tees opened with a locomotive designed by a former colliery engineer pulling a 30-wagon train of coal, flour, and 600 passengers. It was the first public railway to use a steam locomotive for passenger service. Horse-drawn wagons continued to share the line for its first decades.
events.revealBlurb: September 27, 1825 — engineer George Stephenson, his locomotive "Locomotion No. 1." On the opening day Stephenson himself drove the engine, reaching a giddy top speed of 24 km/h. The railway ran until nationalization in 1948.

events.title: Liverpool-Manchester Railway Opens
events.blurb: The world's first inter-city passenger railway line opened with ceremony, carrying dignitaries including the Duke of Wellington on eight parallel trains along a 56-kilometre line linking the port of Liverpool with the cotton-manufacturing centre of Manchester. A parliamentary member, William Huskisson, stepped onto the tracks at a refueling stop and was struck by an oncoming locomotive. He died that evening — the first well-known railway fatality.
events.revealBlurb: September 15, 1830 — designed by George Stephenson. Huskisson is universally regarded as the first prominent casualty of the railway age, though he was not strictly the first railway death. The line ran horse- and steam-hauled freight alongside passengers for its first decades.

events.title: Benz Patents the Motorwagen
events.blurb: A 41-year-old German mechanical engineer filed a patent for a three-wheeled vehicle powered by a single-cylinder internal combustion engine of his own design. The machine, producing about 2/3 of a horsepower, could reach a top speed of 16 km/h. His wife Bertha took it on an unauthorized 106-kilometre cross-country trip two years later without telling him, demonstrating its practicality; the publicity helped launch the commercial automobile industry.
events.revealBlurb: January 29, 1886 — Karl Benz, Mannheim. Bertha's 1888 trip required her to refuel at apothecaries (selling ligroin, a cleaning solvent, as the only available fuel) and improvise brake repairs using her garter as an insulator. Benz's company later merged with Daimler's to form Mercedes-Benz.

events.title: Coca-Cola Invented
events.blurb: An Atlanta pharmacist, a former Confederate officer who had become addicted to morphine following a Civil War injury, mixed a flavoured syrup of coca leaves and kola nuts with carbonated water at a downtown soda fountain and began selling it by the glass as a "brain tonic." The formula initially contained a small amount of cocaine; it was removed in 1903. The modestly popular local beverage grew into the world's most recognized consumer brand.
events.revealBlurb: May 8, 1886 — John Pemberton at Jacobs' Pharmacy, Atlanta. Pemberton sold the formula piecemeal in ill health; Asa Griggs Candler consolidated ownership and built the business. Coca-Cola's secret recipe, "Merchandise 7X," is supposedly known to only two executives at any time.

events.title: Wright Brothers' First Flight
events.blurb: Two American bicycle-shop owners from Dayton, Ohio achieved the first sustained, controlled, powered flight of a heavier-than-air aircraft on a windswept dune at the Outer Banks of North Carolina. The first flight lasted 12 seconds and covered 36 metres — about the wingspan of a modern commercial airliner. They made three more flights that morning; the fourth covered 260 metres in 59 seconds. Few newspapers reported the achievement; commercial aviation took another three decades to arrive.
events.revealBlurb: December 17, 1903 — Orville and Wilbur Wright at Kill Devil Hills, near Kitty Hawk, NC. The flyer is now in the Smithsonian's National Air and Space Museum. The pair spent 4 years after their first flight battling patent disputes and litigation rather than manufacturing planes.

events.title: McCarthy Wheeling Speech
events.blurb: At a Lincoln Day dinner in West Virginia, a previously obscure U.S. senator brandished a piece of paper and claimed it listed 205 known communists working in the State Department. The charge, later revised repeatedly and never substantiated, launched a four-year domestic witch-hunt that would bear his name.
events.revealBlurb: February 9, 1950 — Joseph McCarthy, up for re-election, stumbled onto his signature issue. The "list" he waved kept changing: 205, then 57, then 81. No copy of the original was ever produced. It destroyed thousands of careers anyway.

events.title: Stalin Dies
events.blurb: Found unconscious on the floor of his dacha outside Moscow after a late-night dinner with colleagues, a dictator who had ruled for nearly three decades lingered for four days before dying of a brain hemorrhage. His inner circle, terrified of waking him, had delayed calling doctors for many hours. His state funeral drew crowds so large that dozens were trampled.
events.revealBlurb: March 5, 1953 — Joseph Stalin, 74, at his Kuntsevo dacha. He'd spent the previous evening screening American westerns. His death unleashed a succession struggle; Khrushchev prevailed and began the cautious thaw.

events.title: Suez Crisis
events.blurb: Britain, France, and Israel invaded Egypt to seize the nationalized waterway linking the Mediterranean to the Red Sea. The military operation succeeded; the political one did not. Under combined U.S. and Soviet pressure, the invaders withdrew within two months. The affair is remembered as the moment Britain stopped being a great power.
events.revealBlurb: October 29 to November 7, 1956 — Eisenhower was furious he hadn't been consulted and threatened to sell US holdings of British sterling. British PM Anthony Eden resigned in disgrace three months later. Nasser emerged as the hero of the Arab world.

events.title: Reykjavik Summit
events.blurb: Meeting for two days in a small wooden house in the Icelandic capital, the American and Soviet leaders came astonishingly close to agreeing to eliminate all nuclear weapons within ten years. The talks collapsed over missile defense, and the two men parted grim-faced. But the intellectual groundwork had been laid for an arms-reduction treaty a year later.
events.revealBlurb: October 11-12, 1986 — Reagan and Gorbachev at Höfði House. The property was reputedly haunted. When talks broke down, Gorbachev said privately: "Can you think of any better way out?" Reagan couldn't, and walked to his car.

events.title: Fall of the Berlin Wall
events.blurb: An East German spokesman, reading hastily from a note and misunderstanding its contents, announced at a televised press conference that new travel rules would take effect "immediately." Within hours, tens of thousands of jubilant East Berliners massed at the crossings. Confused border guards, receiving no clear orders, simply let them through. People scrambled onto the concrete barrier with hammers.
events.revealBlurb: November 9, 1989 — the spokesman was Günter Schabowski, who had skimmed the briefing note just before the press conference. Asked when the rules took effect, he shrugged: "As far as I know — immediately." The wall, built in a single night 28 years earlier, came down in a single night too.

events.title: Battle of Crete
events.blurb: For the first time in military history, an entire island was invaded and captured primarily by paratroopers and glider-borne troops alone, dropped onto an enemy-held coastline in the face of fierce resistance. The attackers suffered such catastrophic losses on the opening day that the tactic was never repeated at this scale.
events.revealBlurb: May 20 – June 1, 1941 — Operation Mercury. German paratroopers suffered over 6,500 casualties, including roughly 3,000 killed. Hitler was so shaken he banned future mass airborne operations. The British, Australian, and New Zealand defenders were evacuated; 5,000 were left behind and taken prisoner.

events.title: First Nuclear Chain Reaction
events.blurb: In a squash court beneath a university stadium, a team of physicists assembled 45,000 carefully machined blocks of graphite around pellets of uranium into a lattice the size of a house, withdrew a control rod, and achieved humanity's first self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction — completing the key step toward a new category of weapon.
events.revealBlurb: December 2, 1942, under Stagg Field at the University of Chicago. Enrico Fermi's team celebrated with a bottle of Chianti in paper cups. The coded telegram sent to Washington read: "The Italian navigator has just landed in the New World." The reactor sat in a populated neighbourhood with no containment vessel.

events.title: Me 262's First All-Jet Flight
events.blurb: A swept-wing aircraft climbed away from a Bavarian airfield under pure jet power for the first time, reaching speeds that no piston-engined fighter could match, signalling that the era of propeller-driven military aviation was ending. The technology was real and available — but bureaucratic delays and a leadership obsession with bombers kept it from operational service for more than two years.
events.revealBlurb: July 18, 1942, Leipheim — pilot Fritz Wendel flew the Me 262 V3 on jet power alone for the first time. Hitler later insisted the aircraft be developed as a bomber rather than a fighter, reportedly costing Germany a 14-month delay. When it finally entered service in 1944, it was too little too late: fuel shortages kept most on the ground.

events.title: Yalta Conference
events.blurb: Three heads of government convened at a palatial Crimean resort to decide the political geography of the postwar world — agreeing on the division of a defeated nation into occupation zones, the formation of a new international peace organisation, and the borders of several countries whose populations had no vote in the matter.
events.revealBlurb: February 4–11, 1945. FDR was visibly ill — he would be dead in two months — and Soviet diplomats exploited his eagerness for a deal. Stalin's concessions on free elections in Eastern Europe proved worthless within two years. Churchill reportedly told his doctor: "I do not suppose that at any moment in history has the agony of the world been so great or widespread."

events.title: Victory in Europe Day
events.blurb: Unconditional surrender documents were signed at an Allied headquarters on two successive nights in two different cities, and the moment the ceasefire took effect at one minute past eleven, millions of people in cities across a battered continent poured into the streets to celebrate the end of a conflict that had killed an estimated 70 to 85 million human beings.
events.revealBlurb: May 8, 1945. Germany signed the first surrender at Reims on May 7; a second signing in Berlin satisfied Soviet demands. Stalin proclaimed May 9 as Victory Day — still observed in Russia today. More than a million people celebrated in the streets across the UK. Churchill told the crowds from a Whitehall balcony: "God bless you all. This is your victory."

events.title: British Surrender at Saratoga
events.blurb: A British army of 6,000 men under a genteel general who had marched south from Canada intending to split the American colonies along the Hudson Valley found itself encircled at a rural New York hamlet after two pitched battles and dwindling supplies. The general surrendered his entire force to the American commander. It was the most consequential Allied success of the war; France, which had been secretly aiding the colonies, publicly entered the conflict four months later.
events.revealBlurb: October 17, 1777 — British general John Burgoyne surrenders to American general Horatio Gates. Burgoyne had been marching from Canada; a complementary British push up the Hudson from New York had been misdirected to Pennsylvania. The victory secured French diplomatic recognition and military alliance.

events.title: Franco-American Alliance
events.blurb: A French-American treaty signed in Paris transformed the American rebellion into a global war. France, which had been secretly funneling weapons and volunteers to the rebels through front companies, formally recognized American independence, committed its navy to the war, and in return secured commercial terms with the new republic. Spain joined the next year, the Netherlands the year after, and Britain soon found herself fighting Europe's great powers on multiple oceans.
events.revealBlurb: February 6, 1778 — Treaty of Alliance, Paris. Benjamin Franklin, the Americans' chief diplomat, had worked the French court for two years in a coonskin cap that French aristocrats found exotically charming. France's participation in the war contributed significantly to its own fiscal collapse a decade later.

events.title: Treaty of Paris Recognizes American Independence
events.blurb: Representatives of Britain and the United States signed a peace treaty at a Paris hotel ending the American Revolutionary War. Britain recognized the new country's independence; set its western boundary at the Mississippi River; and granted generous fishing rights off Newfoundland. Spain and France signed separate treaties the same day ending their parallel wars. Britain had lost the largest and richest colony in the world.
events.revealBlurb: September 3, 1783 — Hotel d'York, Paris. American negotiators: Benjamin Franklin, John Adams, John Jay. The United States shrewdly kept its French ally out of the negotiations, violating the Franco-American alliance's terms, and secured better borders as a result.

events.title: U.S. Constitution Signed
events.blurb: Fifty-five delegates meeting for four months in a Philadelphia state house, working in secret through a sweltering summer with the windows closed against spies, produced a seven-article document replacing the loose Articles of Confederation with a stronger federal framework. Thirty-nine of them signed. An 81-year-old Benjamin Franklin, who had been at nearly every session, pointed at the sun carved into George Washington's chair and said he was finally sure it was rising, not setting.
events.revealBlurb: September 17, 1787 — Independence Hall, Philadelphia. Ratified June 21, 1788 after New Hampshire became the ninth state to approve. The Constitution has been amended 27 times in 235 years — less than once per decade. A different Philadelphia-era document, the Bill of Rights, followed in 1791.

events.title: Louisiana Purchase Treaty Signed
events.blurb: American negotiators in Paris signed a treaty acquiring roughly 828,000 square miles of territory from France — doubling the size of the United States — for approximately $15 million, or about three cents per acre. The purchase, which Napoleon offered because he needed cash for his European wars, encompassed all or part of fifteen future states and opened the continent to westward expansion.
events.revealBlurb: April 30, 1803 — Paris. Jefferson had only authorized $10 million and was seeking to buy New Orleans alone; Napoleon offered the entire territory. Jefferson privately wondered whether he had constitutional authority to make the deal at all, but bought it anyway. The full price, with interest, came to about $23 million.

events.title: Avicenna's Canon of Medicine
events.blurb: A 40-year-old Persian polymath in Central Asia completed a five-volume medical encyclopedia synthesizing Greek, Roman, Indian, and Islamic medical knowledge into a single coherent system, with detailed descriptions of diseases, treatments, and pharmaceuticals. Translated into Latin by the 12th century, it became the standard medical textbook of European universities for over five centuries, remaining in use into the early 1700s.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1025 — Ibn Sina (Avicenna). His synthesis included the role of preventive medicine, the value of controlled trials, and notable observations on tuberculosis and diabetes. The Canon's authority in European medical schools lasted longer than Galen's, persisting well into the Enlightenment.

events.title: Aspirin Marketed
events.blurb: A German pharmaceutical and dye company began commercial sales of acetylsalicylic acid tablets under a trade name they had registered, marketed initially as an analgesic and anti-inflammatory. The active compound had been synthesized decades earlier, but this company had developed a stable, pure form suitable for mass production. The drug became one of the best-selling over-the-counter medications in history; low-dose versions are now used preventively against cardiovascular disease.
events.revealBlurb: March 6, 1899 — Bayer AG. Chief chemist Felix Hoffmann is traditionally credited; some historians credit Arthur Eichengrün, a Jewish colleague whose role was erased under Nazi-era Bayer PR. The drug's trade name came from a combination of "acetyl" and Spiraea, a plant source of salicylic acid.

events.title: Banting Discovers Insulin
events.blurb: A 29-year-old Canadian surgeon and a 22-year-old graduate student, working in a borrowed University of Toronto lab through a hot summer, isolated an extract from dog pancreases that, when injected into diabetic dogs, brought their blood sugar back toward normal. By January of the following year, they had injected a 14-year-old boy dying of diabetes; he recovered dramatically. Diabetes, previously a death sentence for type 1 patients, became a manageable chronic disease.
events.revealBlurb: July 27, 1921 — Frederick Banting and Charles Best. Banting and mentor John Macleod shared the 1923 Nobel; Banting split his prize money with Best. The team sold the patent rights to the University of Toronto for one dollar each. Insulin remains a life-saving medication for tens of millions.

events.title: WHO Certifies Smallpox Eradication
events.blurb: The World Health Assembly certified the global eradication of smallpox — the only human infectious disease ever deliberately driven to extinction — following a 13-year WHO campaign using ring vaccination to contain and eliminate every remaining outbreak. The last naturally occurring case had been recorded in Somalia in 1977, ending a disease that had killed an estimated 300 million people in the 20th century alone.

events.title: Human Genome Draft Published
events.blurb: Two groups — the international Human Genome Project consortium and the private company Celera Genomics, which had entered the race late with a competing methodology — simultaneously published their draft sequences of the 3 billion base pairs of the human genome in the journals Nature and Science. The entries were the culmination of 11 years of work and a vast investment of computing and laboratory resources. Humans had roughly 21,000 genes — far fewer than most biologists had predicted.
events.revealBlurb: February 12, 2001 — publications in Nature (consortium) and Science (Celera). The "finished" version of the sequence arrived in 2003. Sequencing a human genome now costs about $200 (down from $2.7 billion) and takes a day.

events.title: Archimedes' Principle of Buoyancy
events.blurb: A Greek mathematician established that an object submerged in fluid is buoyed upward by a force equal to the weight of fluid it displaces — a principle explaining why objects float or sink and allowing the density of irregular objects to be measured precisely. The insight reportedly struck the mathematician while stepping into a bath, causing him to run through the streets in excitement.
events.revealBlurb: c. 250 BCE — the "Eureka" bath story was first told by the Roman writer Vitruvius about 200 years after Archimedes lived, so historians treat it sceptically. What is not disputed is that Archimedes wrote it all down carefully in On Floating Bodies, one of the oldest surviving works of physics. He also calculated an approximation of pi accurate to three decimal places.

events.title: Galileo Maps the Moon
events.blurb: An Italian natural philosopher directed a 20× magnification tube skyward and produced detailed drawings of the Moon's surface, revealing mountains and craters rather than a perfect celestial sphere as ancient philosophy held. He calculated the heights of lunar mountains by measuring the lengths of the shadows they cast.

events.title: Newton's Principia Published
events.blurb: A three-volume work laid out universal laws of motion and gravitation in mathematical form, explaining why apples fall and why planets orbit in ellipses with a single unified framework. The laws held that every mass in the universe attracts every other mass with a force proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of their distance.
events.revealBlurb: July 5, 1687 — Edmond Halley paid for the printing out of his own pocket after the Royal Society spent its book budget on a history of fishes. Newton later said a dispute over priority with Robert Hooke was the reason he almost withheld the whole thing.

events.title: Photoelectric Effect Explained
events.blurb: A paper explained why shining light on a metal surface ejects electrons only when the light exceeds a threshold frequency — never for very bright low-frequency light — by proposing that light itself travels in discrete energy packets rather than continuous waves. The finding resolved a long-standing paradox and extended the quantum idea from heat radiation to light, fundamentally changing the understanding of what light is.
events.revealBlurb: June 9, 1905 — this was the paper that explicitly won Einstein the 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics, not relativity. When the Nobel Committee finally awarded it (sixteen years late), they cited this discovery specifically. Einstein reportedly joked that the committee must have found relativity too controversial.

events.title: Gravitational Waves Detected
events.blurb: Two massive laser interferometers simultaneously detected a brief chirp of spacetime distortion that lasted a fraction of a second — the gravitational ripple produced by two black holes colliding 1.3 billion light-years away. The signal exactly matched the prediction of general relativity and confirmed that spacetime itself can vibrate, opening a new branch of observational astronomy.
events.revealBlurb: Detected September 14, 2015; announced February 11, 2016 — the team waited five months to check for errors. The signal lasted 0.2 seconds. One scientist described hearing the chirp played as audio as "nature singing to us." Three founders of LIGO — Weiss, Barish, and Thorne — shared the 2017 Nobel Prize in Physics.

events.title: Bayeux Tapestry Completed
events.blurb: An embroidered strip of linen 70 metres long and 50 centimetres high, worked in coloured wool yarns, depicts in 58 scenes the Norman conquest of a cross-Channel kingdom — the diplomatic prelude, the invasion fleet, a victorious battle, and the death of a king by arrow. It includes 623 human figures, 202 horses, 55 dogs, and a Latin commentary running across the top.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1077 — commissioned either by Bishop Odo of Bayeux or Queen Matilda. Despite its name, it is technically embroidery, not tapestry. It survived the French Revolution only because a local lawyer hid it when a crowd tried to use it to cover an ammunition wagon.

events.title: The Last Supper Completed
events.blurb: An Italian polymath completed a 9-metre-wide mural in the refectory of a Dominican convent in a northern Italian city, depicting Christ announcing his betrayal and the instant of shocked reaction on the faces of his twelve disciples. The artist had worked on it for three years, painting in oil on a dry wall rather than true fresco — a choice that made the picture deteriorate visibly within his own lifetime.
events.revealBlurb: 1498 — Leonardo da Vinci in Santa Maria delle Grazie, Milan. His experimental technique began flaking within 20 years. The painting has been restored many times, most recently between 1978 and 1999. Allied bombing in 1943 destroyed the refectory roof but the wall survived.

events.title: Mona Lisa Stolen
events.blurb: An Italian handyman who had worked at a Paris museum hid overnight in a storage closet, walked out the next morning in his worker's smock carrying a 77 by 53 cm wooden panel under his arm, and disappeared for two years and four months. The panel was a portrait by Leonardo da Vinci of a Florentine merchant's wife. The theft made worldwide news; Picasso and the poet Apollinaire were briefly questioned as suspects. The picture had been little known until this moment.
events.revealBlurb: August 21, 1911 — Vincenzo Peruggia. He was caught in Florence 28 months later trying to sell it to the Uffizi. He served seven months in Italian prison and was celebrated as a patriot by many Italians. The theft made the Mona Lisa internationally famous.

events.title: Armory Show Opens
events.blurb: An exhibition at a New York National Guard armory introduced American audiences to European modernism at industrial scale — 1,300 paintings and sculptures by artists most had never heard of, including Matisse, Picasso, Duchamp, and Brancusi. Duchamp's "Nude Descending a Staircase No. 2" was ridiculed by a popular cartoonist as "explosion in a shingle factory" and drew crowds for exactly that reason. The show moved on to Chicago and Boston and is credited with changing the course of American art.
events.revealBlurb: February 17 to March 15, 1913 — the 69th Regiment Armory, Lexington Avenue, NYC. Around 90,000 people visited in New York alone. Theodore Roosevelt wrote a mostly-baffled review; a reproduction of the "Nude" was burned in effigy at the Chicago Art Institute.

events.title: Warhol's Campbell's Soup Cans
events.blurb: A 33-year-old former commercial illustrator exhibited 32 canvases, each showing a single can of condensed soup — one for each of the 32 varieties the food company then sold. He had painted them by projecting photographic images onto the canvas and tracing. The show sold modestly: five of the canvases went for $100 each; the gallery owner bought them back and later resold the whole set for $2 million.
events.revealBlurb: July 9, 1962 — Ferus Gallery, Los Angeles, Andy Warhol. The artist said he ate Campbell's soup every day for 20 years. The set is now in MoMA. Warhol would soon apply the same silk-screen methods to Marilyn Monroe, Jackie Kennedy, and Elvis.

events.title: Bicycle Thieves Released
events.blurb: An Italian director released a quiet 89-minute film about an unemployed working-class man whose stolen bicycle means he cannot take a new job pasting posters on walls. The non-professional actors, documentary-style camera, and refusal of melodramatic conventions defined the Italian neorealist movement. The film spoke for a generation of post-war European audiences who had had enough of Hollywood glamour.
events.revealBlurb: November 24, 1948 — Vittorio De Sica. The father was played by a real factory worker; the son by a young boy De Sica spotted on the street. It won an honorary Academy Award before the foreign language category existed. Its influence on later directors — from Ken Loach to Satyajit Ray — is enormous.

events.title: Breathless Released
events.blurb: A 29-year-old French film critic turned director released a 90-minute crime film about a petty thief on the run in Paris with his American girlfriend, shot on handheld camera using natural light, jump cuts, and improvised dialogue. The film's insouciant rulebreaking embodied a new generation of European filmmaking, christened the "Nouvelle Vague" by a critic five years earlier. It made its star into the archetype of post-war cool.
events.revealBlurb: March 16, 1960 — Jean-Luc Godard, starring Jean-Paul Belmondo and Jean Seberg. The famously jarring jump-cuts emerged from an editing crisis: the film was too long and Godard simply removed shots rather than shorten scenes.

events.title: Fellini's 8½ Released
events.blurb: An Italian director released a semi-autobiographical film about a filmmaker suffering a creative block while preparing his next picture, in which the director's own memories, dreams, and erotic fantasies dissolve into the plot he is trying to construct. The Italian title referred literally to the number of films the director had made. It won two Oscars and became the classic film-about-film-making, endlessly quoted by later directors similarly stuck.
events.revealBlurb: February 14, 1963 — Federico Fellini, with Marcello Mastroianni as his alter ego. Fellini had genuinely been blocked after a string of successes; the film emerged from trying to work out why. It was remade as a Broadway musical ("Nine") in 1982.

events.title: Jaws Released
events.blurb: A 28-year-old director released a 124-minute thriller about a great white shark terrorizing a New England beach resort. Principal photography, supposed to last 55 days, ran 159; the mechanical shark broke down constantly and was rarely shown, producing the film's signature off-screen menace. Released across a record number of screens nationwide with a saturation TV ad campaign, it invented the summer blockbuster.
events.revealBlurb: June 20, 1975 — Steven Spielberg. The shark's malfunctions forced Spielberg to rely on John Williams' two-note score to telegraph the threat. The film caused a measurable drop in US beach attendance for years afterward.

events.title: Parasite Wins Best Picture
events.blurb: A 50-year-old South Korean director's satirical thriller about a poor family insinuating itself into a wealthy family's household became the first non-English-language film to win the top prize at a major U.S. film awards ceremony. It also took Best Director, Best Original Screenplay, and Best International Feature — a quadruple sweep by a "foreign" film that industry observers had long thought impossible. The director thanked Martin Scorsese in one of his acceptance speeches.
events.revealBlurb: February 9, 2020 — Bong Joon-ho's "Parasite" at the 92nd Academy Awards. The film's Korean-language narrative beat Sam Mendes's "1917" and Tarantino's "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood." It was also the first Palme d'Or winner to win Best Picture in 65 years.

events.title: Ashoka Conquers Kalinga
events.blurb: A Mauryan emperor's army conquered a fiercely resistant coastal kingdom after a war that, by the emperor's own inscriptions, killed 100,000 people and displaced 150,000 more. Revolted by the carnage he had ordered, the emperor publicly renounced war, embraced a philosophy of non-violence, and had pillars erected across his realm inscribed with edicts of compassion — the earliest dateable Indian texts we can read today.
events.revealBlurb: c. 261 BCE — Ashoka the Great, Maurya dynasty. The lion capital from his pillar at Sarnath — four lions standing back to back — is now India's national emblem.

events.title: Rajendra Chola's Navy Crosses the Bay of Bengal
events.blurb: The Chola emperor dispatched a fleet from the Coromandel Coast that crossed the Bay of Bengal, sacked the capital of the Srivijaya empire in Sumatra, captured its king, seized cities along the Malay Peninsula, and imposed Chola trading dominance over the sea lanes between India and China. It was the largest seaborne military operation ever launched from the Indian subcontinent, covering over 3,000 kilometres of open ocean.
events.revealBlurb: 1025 CE — Rajendra Chola I, Tamil Nadu. For the next century, Tamil merchant guilds — the Manigramam and Ainnurruvar — dominated trade from the Malabar coast to present-day Singapore. This is the moment when South India owned the Indian Ocean.

events.title: Qutb-ud-Din Aibak Founds the Delhi Sultanate
events.blurb: A Turkic slave-soldier who had risen to command the armies of the Ghurid empire in India declared himself Sultan of Delhi after his master was assassinated in Central Asia. This man — who had been purchased as a child in a Nishapur slave market — now controlled the largest political entity in the subcontinent. He commissioned what would become one of India's most visited monuments, the Qutb Minar in Delhi, before dying four years later in a polo accident.
events.revealBlurb: 1206 CE — Qutb-ud-Din Aibak, first Sultan of Delhi. He was known as "Lakhbaksh" (giver of lakhs) for his generosity. The Qutb Minar he began stands 73 metres tall and remains the tallest brick minaret in the world over 800 years later.

events.title: Akbar Secures the Mughal Throne
events.blurb: A 13-year-old Mughal prince was crowned emperor at Kalanaur, Punjab, moments after his father fell down a library staircase in Delhi. His regent Bairam Khan immediately faced a formidable rival — the Hindu general Hemu, who had taken Delhi with 30,000 cavalry and 1,500 war elephants. At the second Battle of Panipat, Hemu was felled by a stray arrow mid-battle, his army collapsed, and the boy king's empire was saved.
events.revealBlurb: February 1556 CE — Akbar the Great. The same king who would later abolish the jizya tax, marry Rajput princesses, invent a syncretic religion, and reportedly have three thousand women in his harem started his reign as a frightened teenager hiding behind his general.

events.title: Guru Arjan Dev Is Executed by Mughal Order
events.blurb: The fifth Sikh Guru, who had compiled the Adi Granth and built the Golden Temple, was arrested by the Mughal emperor on charges of blessing a rebel prince. Ordered to pay a fine of 200,000 rupees and alter his scripture's hymns, he refused both. He was then tortured over several days — made to sit on a burning iron plate while red-hot sand was poured over his body — and died in Lahore. His execution permanently changed the relationship between the Sikh Panth and Mughal power.
events.revealBlurb: May 30, 1606 CE — Guru Arjan Dev Ji, Lahore, Mughal Empire under Jahangir. His martyrdom led his successor, Guru Hargobind, to take up two swords — one of spiritual authority, one of temporal power — and build an armed Sikh army.

events.title: Mosaic Browser Released
events.blurb: Undergraduate students at a University of Illinois supercomputing centre released a graphical web browser for Unix, with a version for Windows and Mac released later in the year. Unlike the earlier terminal-based browsers, it could display images inline with text. Within 18 months, web traffic had grown by 10,000 percent. The browser's lead developer would leave to co-found a company that would dominate the next phase.
events.revealBlurb: April 22, 1993 — developed at the NCSA, lead developer Marc Andreessen. Andreessen co-founded Netscape within a year. Mosaic was free for non-commercial use, a decision that gave the web the critical mass it needed.

events.title: eBay Founded
events.blurb: A 28-year-old Iranian-American software engineer set up an online auction site over the Labor Day weekend, initially as a hobby project on a personal server. One of the first items sold was a broken laser pointer for $14.83. When he emailed the buyer to check whether he understood it was broken, the buyer replied that he collected broken laser pointers. The founder realized he had a business on his hands.
events.revealBlurb: September 3, 1995 — Pierre Omidyar. He originally named it AuctionWeb; renamed eBay in 1997, short for Echo Bay Technology, his consulting firm. The first commission was sent as a personal check for $241.19.

events.title: Facebook Launched
events.blurb: A 19-year-old Harvard sophomore with a history of making unauthorized student-directory sites launched, from his dorm room, a social network restricted to students with harvard.edu email addresses. It reached half the Harvard student body within two weeks. He expanded to Yale, Columbia, and Stanford within weeks. Within a year he had dropped out; within four he was a billionaire on paper.
events.revealBlurb: February 4, 2004 — Mark Zuckerberg at Harvard, with co-founders Eduardo Saverin, Andrew McCollum, Dustin Moskovitz, and Chris Hughes. Originally thefacebook.com. Zuckerberg settled with the Winklevoss twins for $65 million in 2008; they spent it on Bitcoin.

events.title: Instagram Launched
events.blurb: A two-person startup released a free iOS app that let users take photos, apply one of eleven retro filters, and share them to a simple timeline-based social network. It acquired 25,000 users on launch day and its first million within three months. Facebook bought the company for $1 billion in cash and stock eighteen months later, when it had thirteen employees and zero revenue.
events.revealBlurb: October 6, 2010 — Kevin Systrom and Mike Krieger. Originally built as a location-based check-in app called Burbn. The $1 billion Facebook acquisition in April 2012 is now considered one of the great bargains in tech history.

events.title: Cambridge Analytica Scandal
events.blurb: A former employee of a small British political consultancy went public with allegations that the firm had harvested personal data from some 87 million Facebook users, mostly without their knowledge or consent, and used it to build psychographic voter-targeting models for the 2016 U.S. presidential and UK Brexit campaigns. Facebook's stock lost $100 billion in market value in ten days. Its CEO was subsequently hauled before the U.S. Congress and the European Parliament.
events.revealBlurb: March 17, 2018 — whistleblower Christopher Wylie in The Observer and New York Times. Cambridge Analytica went bankrupt within two months. Facebook was later fined $5 billion by the U.S. FTC — the largest fine ever for a privacy violation, but about a month's profit for the company.

events.title: Charlemagne Crowned Emperor
events.blurb: A Frankish king, in a papal basilica in the old western imperial capital for Christmas Mass, rose from prayer to be unexpectedly crowned "Emperor of the Romans" by the pope. The coronation resurrected, at least in title, a western empire that had been extinct for 324 years, and established a relationship between popes and emperors that would shape European politics for eight centuries.
events.revealBlurb: December 25, 800 — Charlemagne in Rome, crowned by Pope Leo III. Charlemagne later claimed he had been surprised — but the pope probably wouldn't have dared without his consent. The Holy Roman Empire survived in one form or another until 1806.

events.title: Council of Clermont
events.blurb: The pope, addressing a crowd of French clergy and nobles in an open field outside a central French city after a church council, called on Christendom to take up arms and march east to recover a holy land from Muslim rule. "Deus vult," the crowd cried back — "God wills it." Within three years, 100,000 pilgrims and knights would be on the road.
events.revealBlurb: November 27, 1095 — Pope Urban II. His stated goals shifted in each retelling; the Byzantine emperor had only asked for mercenaries. The First Crusade's armies would surprise everyone, including themselves, by actually reaching Jerusalem.

events.title: Mongol Sack of Baghdad
events.blurb: A Mongol army under a grandson of Genghis Khan besieged a Mesopotamian capital that had been the cultural and financial center of the Islamic world for five centuries. The city fell after thirteen days. The caliph was wrapped in a carpet and trampled by horses; the House of Wisdom was burned. Witnesses said the Tigris ran black for days with the ink of destroyed books, then red with the blood of their authors.
events.revealBlurb: February 10, 1258 — Hulagu Khan. Estimates of the dead range from 90,000 to over a million. The Abbasid Caliphate as a political power died with the city; Islamic civilization's center of gravity shifted permanently to Cairo and later Constantinople.

events.title: Black Death Reaches Europe
events.blurb: A plague arriving by trade galley at a Sicilian port spread through Mediterranean shipping lanes and overland caravans until, over the next five years, it killed an estimated 30-60 percent of Europe's population — perhaps 50 million people. Physicians had no effective response; flagellant processions and mass pogroms of Jews did little but spread the disease faster.
events.revealBlurb: October 1347 — Messina, Sicily. Caused by Yersinia pestis, spread by the fleas of black rats. Wages for surviving laborers roughly doubled; labor scarcity began eroding feudal obligations. The plague cycled back every decade or so for the next three centuries.

events.title: Fall of Granada
events.blurb: The last Muslim ruler of an Andalusian emirate, besieged for seven months in his Alhambra palace, handed over its keys to Castilian and Aragonese monarchs and rode into exile, reportedly sighing at his final view from a mountain pass. The surrender ended 781 years of Muslim political presence on the Iberian peninsula. The same monarchs, three months later, would commission an Italian sailor to seek a western route to Asia.
events.revealBlurb: January 2, 1492 — Ferdinand and Isabella accept the surrender of Muhammad XII (Boabdil). His mother is said to have told him: "You weep like a woman for what you could not defend like a man." Columbus was at the Alhambra that summer presenting his proposal.

events.title: 13th Amendment Ratified
events.blurb: The first of three Reconstruction-era amendments was ratified eight months after a brutal civil war ended, abolishing slavery and involuntary servitude throughout the United States except as punishment for crime. The exception clause would become the legal scaffolding for convict-leasing systems that reproduced plantation labor for another 80 years.
events.revealBlurb: December 6, 1865 — when Georgia became the 27th state to ratify. Mississippi officially ratified only in 1995, and didn't certify it until 2013, due to a paperwork oversight.

events.title: NAACP Founded
events.blurb: A biracial group of activists, scholars, and newspaper editors met at a New York conference on the centennial of Abraham Lincoln's birth to establish an organization dedicated to fighting racial discrimination through legal action and public advocacy. W.E.B. Du Bois, the Harvard-trained sociologist, edited its magazine The Crisis; its lawyers would eventually argue Brown v. Board of Education.
events.revealBlurb: February 12, 1909 — National Association for the Advancement of Colored People. It was founded partly in response to the Springfield, Illinois race riot the year before. Du Bois served as editor of The Crisis for 24 years.

events.title: Tulsa Race Massacre
events.blurb: An armed white mob, deputized by local police and in some cases flown in biplanes to drop makeshift bombs, attacked an affluent Black neighborhood in an Oklahoma oil city nicknamed "Black Wall Street." Over 18 hours they burned 35 blocks of homes and businesses, killed an estimated 100 to 300 residents, and arrested 6,000 survivors. Nobody was ever prosecuted.
events.revealBlurb: May 31 to June 1, 1921 — Greenwood District, Tulsa. The massacre was scrubbed from local newspapers and school curricula for 75 years. A state commission finally investigated in 2001. Mass graves are still being exhumed.

events.title: Executive Order 8802
events.blurb: Facing a threatened mass march on Washington organized by a prominent Black labor leader, a U.S. president signed an executive order banning racial discrimination in the defense industry and federal government. It was the first federal action against employment discrimination since Reconstruction. The threatened march was called off; the larger March would come 22 years later.
events.revealBlurb: June 25, 1941 — Franklin Roosevelt, pushed by A. Philip Randolph. Randolph had assembled 100,000 marchers and refused to call it off without the order. The order created the Fair Employment Practice Committee — a template for later civil rights enforcement.

events.title: Martin Luther King Jr. Assassinated
events.blurb: Stepping onto the balcony outside Room 306 of a Tennessee motel where he was staying while supporting a sanitation workers' strike, the country's most prominent civil rights leader was shot once with a high-powered rifle from across the street. He died an hour later at a nearby hospital. He was 39. Riots broke out in more than 100 American cities within hours of the news.
events.revealBlurb: April 4, 1968 — Lorraine Motel, Memphis. His killer, escaped convict James Earl Ray, was captured in London two months later. The night before, King had ended a speech with: "I've been to the mountaintop. I may not get there with you, but we, as a people, will get to the Promised Land."

events.title: Oprah's "You Get a Car!"
events.blurb: An American daytime talk-show host opened her show's 19th-season premiere by giving a brand-new compact sedan to each of 276 audience members who, she said, had been nominated by loved ones as desperately needing a new vehicle. She turned to a different audience section and shouted: "You get a car! You get a car!" each audience member in turn. The sustained joy — and the full-volume shouting — became a lasting cultural moment captured in countless memes and parodies.
events.revealBlurb: September 13, 2004 — Oprah Winfrey on The Oprah Winfrey Show. The cars were Pontiac G6 sedans donated by General Motors, which covered the ~$7 million cost as a promotion. Audience members were reportedly shocked to discover the IRS expected them to pay tax on the "gift" of around $7,000.

events.title: YouTube Launched
events.blurb: Three former PayPal employees, reportedly frustrated that they couldn't easily share a video of a dinner party or (by an alternate legend) a wardrobe malfunction from a recent sporting event, registered a domain name for a video-sharing site. The site's first uploaded video, "Me at the zoo," was an 18-second clip of one of the founders standing in front of elephants at the San Diego Zoo. Google bought them for $1.65 billion in stock twenty months later.
events.revealBlurb: February 14, 2005 — Chad Hurley, Steve Chen, Jawed Karim. The "Me at the zoo" video is still online, with over 350 million views. Users now upload over 500 hours of video every minute.

events.title: Britney Shaves Her Head
events.blurb: A 25-year-old American pop star walked into a Los Angeles hair salon at 8 PM, asked a stylist to shave her head completely, and when the stylist refused, picked up the electric clippers and did it herself. Paparazzi captured the scene through the salon window. Images went global within hours, becoming an emblem of a period of intensely public personal struggle — divorce, custody battles, reportage, and tabloid harassment. She would be placed under conservatorship nine months later.
events.revealBlurb: February 16, 2007 — Britney Spears at Esther's Haircutting Studio, Tarzana, CA. The conservatorship lasted 13 years, ending in November 2021 after the #FreeBritney movement. Her 2023 memoir "The Woman in Me" describes the head-shaving as a reaction to feeling over-managed and pressured by the industry.

events.title: Robin Williams Dies
events.blurb: A 63-year-old American actor and comedian was found dead at his home in California's Marin County, having died by suicide. An autopsy later revealed he had been suffering from Lewy body dementia — a form of dementia that causes visual hallucinations and movement problems — that had been misdiagnosed as Parkinson's disease during his lifetime. His widow wrote afterwards that the real disease had been terrifying him; she called it "the terrorist in my husband's brain."
events.revealBlurb: August 11, 2014 — Robin Williams. His final film "Night at the Museum: Secret of the Tomb" was released posthumously in December. Williams had won an Academy Award for "Good Will Hunting" (1997); his improvised standup, Mork & Mindy, Mrs. Doubtfire, Aladdin, and Dead Poets Society span a career of enormous generosity toward audiences.

events.title: "The Dress" Goes Viral
events.blurb: A 21-year-old Scottish woman posted a photograph of a dress on her Tumblr account asking for help settling a family argument — was it black and blue, or white and gold? The photo went viral overnight. Approximately 40 percent of viewers saw it as white and gold; 50 percent as black and blue. Vision scientists spent months examining why. The actual dress, in real life, was black and blue. The phenomenon became a landmark case study in how individual visual perception varies based on assumptions about ambient lighting.
events.revealBlurb: February 26, 2015 — Cecilia Bleasdale's photograph, posted by Caitlin McNeill. Roman Originals, who made the dress, saw a 560 percent spike in sales. Neuroscientists published papers on it for years. It revived serious research into color constancy and top-down visual processing.

events.title: Attack on Pearl Harbor
events.blurb: At 7:55 that morning, 353 Imperial Japanese aircraft struck the U.S. naval base at Pearl Harbor, Hawaii, sinking or damaging 19 ships including eight battleships and destroying 188 aircraft in under two hours. The attack killed 2,403 Americans — including 1,177 sailors and Marines aboard the USS Arizona, which exploded catastrophically and sank in nine minutes.
events.revealBlurb: December 7, 1941 — Pearl Harbor, Oahu. The USS Arizona still lies on the harbor floor; approximately 900 of her crew remain entombed inside. The declaration of war passed Congress the next day, 470–1 — the single dissenting vote was from pacifist Representative Jeannette Rankin of Montana.

events.title: Fall of Singapore
events.blurb: An island fortress considered impregnable from the sea fell in one week when attackers crossed a narrow strait at its land-facing back and advanced down a peninsula faster than anyone had thought possible. The surrender of 80,000 troops in a single capitulation stands as the largest in the history of the British Army.
events.revealBlurb: February 15, 1942. General Percival surrendered at 6:20 PM. Churchill called it "the worst disaster and largest capitulation in British history." The great naval guns of Singapore pointed seaward and many lacked armour-piercing shells anyway — the attack had come from the wrong direction entirely.

events.title: Dieppe Raid
events.blurb: Roughly 6,000 troops — mostly Canadians — landed in daylight on a heavily defended beach overlooked by cliffs and were cut down before many could clear the waterline, suffering nearly 60 percent casualties in under ten hours. Planners later claimed the catastrophic failure provided lessons that saved countless lives in subsequent amphibious operations.
events.revealBlurb: August 19, 1942 — Operation Jubilee. Of 4,963 Canadians who embarked, only 2,210 returned to England; 907 were killed and 1,946 taken prisoner. The Germans, who had received advance intelligence, held their positions with minimal effort. Churchill admitted privately it was "a very heavy and grievous loss."

events.title: Operation Torch Landings
events.blurb: American forces entered the ground war for the first time, landing simultaneously at three points along a North African coastline controlled by a French administration that had to decide within hours whether to fight the new arrivals or join them against a common enemy. The simultaneous approach from both directions trapped an entire Axis army between closing forces.
events.revealBlurb: November 8, 1942 — the first major American offensive operation of the war in the European theatre. French commanders initially resisted; Vichy French forces fired on US troops and sank a destroyer. A ceasefire was agreed three days later on November 11 — the 24th anniversary of the World War I Armistice.

events.title: Tehran Conference
events.blurb: The three most powerful leaders of the opposing alliance met for the first time in a capital city in southwest Asia, committing to a firm timeline for a massive cross-channel invasion in spring, agreeing on the postwar borders of one eastern European nation, and beginning to sketch the political shape of the world that would follow the conflict.
events.revealBlurb: November 28 – December 1, 1943 — FDR, Churchill, and Stalin met in Tehran. It was the first time FDR and Stalin met in person. Roosevelt, whose security staff feared assassination, moved into the Soviet Embassy at Stalin's suggestion — and Soviet intelligence promptly bugged his suite. Churchill celebrated his 69th birthday at the conference with a dinner attended by all three leaders.

events.title: Kismet Released
events.blurb: A Bombay Talkies crime film with an unambiguous anti-hero — the lead character is a thief and a cad — opened in the depths of winter during a bitter internal dispute that was tearing the studio apart, yet became the first film in Indian cinema history to gross ₹1 crore. At a Calcutta cinema it ran for 187 consecutive weeks, a record that stood for 32 years.
events.revealBlurb: January 9, 1943, Bombay. Directed by Gyan Mukherjee, starring Ashok Kumar. Its patriotic song "Door Hato Ae Duniyawalon" — aimed at colonial occupation without naming it — spread through cities as independence agitation intensified. The British censors initially approved it without grasping the subtext.

events.title: Pyaasa Released
events.blurb: A poet who the city believes to be dead wanders through venal publishers and indifferent relatives in a film Guru Dutt both directed and starred in, constructing one of Indian cinema's most sustained indictments of commercialised culture through Sahir Ludhianvi's Urdu verse set to S.D. Burman's music. Time magazine later placed it among the 100 greatest films ever made.
events.revealBlurb: February 22, 1957 — Guru Dutt's masterwork. The film was semi-autobiographical; Dutt was increasingly alienated from the Bombay film industry's values, an estrangement he did not survive — he died in 1964, aged 39. The song "Jaane Woh Kaise Log The" remains among the most covered in Hindi film music.

events.title: Anand Released
events.blurb: A terminally ill man facing lymphosarcoma of the intestine spends his remaining months arguing that life is worth celebrating — while his doctor-friend records him in a notebook — in a film whose two leads delivered career-defining performances on opposite emotional registers. Its final line, spoken after death, became among the most quoted in Hindi cinema.
events.revealBlurb: March 12, 1971 — directed by Hrishikesh Mukherjee, dialogues by Gulzar. Rajesh Khanna was at the absolute peak of his popularity; Amitabh Bachchan was still a supporting player. The film reportedly made Amitabh Bachchan weep on set during the final sequence — which Mukherjee kept in the film.

events.title: Sholay Released
events.blurb: A three-hour curry Western about two small-time criminals hired by a retired policeman to hunt a ruthless dacoit opened on India's Independence Day to a tepid first week before word-of-mouth turned it into the longest-running Indian film of all time. It played uninterrupted at a single Bombay theatre for five and a half years — 286 consecutive weeks.
events.revealBlurb: August 15, 1975. Director Ramesh Sippy. Amjad Khan as Gabbar Singh was nearly replaced because the scriptwriter thought his voice was too thin. The original ending showed Thakur killing Gabbar with spiked shoes — the censor board forced a reshoot. "Kitne aadmi the?" became a national catchphrase.

events.title: Slumdog Millionaire Wins Best Picture
events.blurb: A British-directed film set entirely in Mumbai — shot partly in the Dharavi slum with non-professional child actors, partly in the chaos of the city's streets — swept eight Oscars including Best Picture at the 81st Academy Awards, making it the first film primarily set and cast in India to win the top prize. Its pavement-to-riches structure was lifted directly from Bollywood's own playbook.
events.revealBlurb: February 22, 2009. Directed by Danny Boyle. A.R. Rahman won Best Original Score and Best Original Song for "Jai Ho" — his first Oscars, received in the same night. The child actors from the film were discovered to be living in poverty after production wrapped, triggering international headlines.

events.title: Brunelleschi's Dome Completed
events.blurb: A Florentine goldsmith turned architect completed, after 16 years of work without scaffolding, a vast octagonal dome over the crossing of a century-old cathedral. The double-shelled design, assembled with four million bricks in a self-supporting herringbone pattern, spanned 42 metres — wider than any dome built since Roman antiquity. The cathedral had stood domeless for over a century, waiting for someone to figure out how.
events.revealBlurb: August 25, 1436 — consecrated. Filippo Brunelleschi at Santa Maria del Fiore, Florence. He refused to leave blueprints, fearing competitors would steal the ideas. Part of the technique was rediscovered only in the 20th century through forensic study of the bricks.

events.title: Gutenberg Bible Completed
events.blurb: A German goldsmith completed printing a 1,286-page Latin Bible using a press with movable metal type, producing an estimated 180 copies at a rate no scribe could approach. Each sheet required individually set letter blocks cast in an alloy of lead, tin, and antimony — making it the first book in Europe produced by mechanical movable type.

events.title: Gutenberg Bible Printed
events.blurb: A goldsmith in a Rhine-valley city completed the first book printed in Europe using movable metal type — a Latin Bible set in 42 lines per page, bound in 180 copies. His press combined existing technologies — oil-based ink, a wine-press frame, cast-metal punches — into an invention that would be blamed for everything from the Reformation to the Renaissance to modern literacy.
events.revealBlurb: 1455 — Johannes Gutenberg in Mainz. Forty-nine copies are known to survive; roughly twenty are complete. Gutenberg himself was sued by his financier the same year and lost the press.

events.title: Cortés Reaches Tenochtitlán
events.blurb: A 34-year-old Spanish conquistador, in defiance of orders from the governor of Cuba who had tried to recall him, entered the causeway-linked lakeside capital of the Aztec Triple Alliance — a city of perhaps 200,000 people, one of the largest in the world, built on an island in a high-altitude lake. The Aztec emperor met him with courtesy, gifts, and quiet suspicion. Within two years the emperor would be dead and the city in ruins.
events.revealBlurb: November 8, 1519 — Hernán Cortés meets Moctezuma II in Tenochtitlán (modern Mexico City). The Spanish force was about 500 strong, augmented by thousands of Tlaxcalan allies who hated the Aztecs. Cortés had burned his own ships on the coast to prevent desertion.

events.title: Edict of Nantes
events.blurb: The first Bourbon king of France, a former Protestant who had converted to Catholicism to secure his crown ("Paris is worth a Mass"), issued an edict guaranteeing Protestant Huguenots freedom of worship in specific towns, civil equality, and the right to maintain their own fortified places. The compromise ended 36 years of Wars of Religion and was the most expansive grant of religious toleration any European state had yet made. His grandson would revoke it 87 years later.
events.revealBlurb: April 13, 1598 — Henry IV of France. Louis XIV revoked it in 1685, triggering a Protestant exodus of perhaps 400,000 skilled workers. Henry IV himself was assassinated by a Catholic fanatic in 1610.

events.title: ENIAC Unveiled
events.blurb: Engineers at an American university publicly demonstrated an 27-tonne general-purpose electronic computer, filling a 30 by 15 metre room with 17,468 vacuum tubes, 10,000 capacitors, and 6,000 switches. The machine calculated artillery-shell trajectories 2,400 times faster than a human with an adding machine. Programming it required physically rewiring hundreds of cables; the programmers — all women — had to crawl inside to swap plugs.
events.revealBlurb: February 15, 1946 — University of Pennsylvania. Designers J. Presper Eckert and John Mauchly. Programmers: Kay McNulty, Betty Jennings, Betty Snyder, Marlyn Wescoff, Fran Bilas, and Ruth Lichterman. They were not invited to the unveiling dinner; their faces were cropped out of celebratory photos for decades.

events.title: Apple Computer Founded
events.blurb: Two 20-something Californians, a college dropout and a self-taught engineer, formed a partnership to sell a printed-circuit-board computer design the engineer had developed and the dropout had realized was marketable. A third partner, older and more cautious, asked out within two weeks and sold his share back for $800. The initial product was a hand-built board requiring the buyer to supply their own power supply, keyboard, and case.
events.revealBlurb: April 1, 1976 — Steve Jobs, Steve Wozniak, and Ronald Wayne. Wayne's 10 percent share would today be worth over $300 billion. He has said he doesn't regret selling out; he'd been in a startup before and wanted to avoid another personal-liability exposure.

events.title: iPhone Announced
events.blurb: A California computer company's co-founder unveiled a new class of mobile phone at a San Francisco conference, combining a widescreen iPod, a mobile internet browser, and a phone into a single slim device controlled entirely by a multi-touch finger-driven screen. He dialled a coffee shop on stage to demonstrate. Nokia's executives watching the announcement reportedly laughed at its lack of a physical keyboard; BlackBerry's CEO later admitted they also underestimated it.
events.revealBlurb: January 9, 2007 — Steve Jobs at Macworld. It went on sale June 29. The original did not support 3G, had no copy-and-paste, and shipped without an App Store — those all came in subsequent years. Apple now makes over $200 billion a year just from iPhones.

events.title: Watson Wins Jeopardy
events.blurb: An IBM supercomputer named after the company's founder competed over three nights of a televised American trivia game show against the two greatest human champions the show had ever produced — and won by a wide margin. The machine had been fed a corpus of Wikipedia, encyclopedias, and dictionaries; it processed buzzer-triggered natural-language clues with a complex pipeline of heuristics and statistical models. It was not a single breakthrough; it was an engineering triumph.
events.revealBlurb: February 14-16, 2011 — Watson vs. Ken Jennings and Brad Rutter. Jennings' final written answer on night three: "I, for one, welcome our new computer overlords." IBM spent heavily trying to commercialize Watson for healthcare and business; most of those products have since been divested or discontinued.

events.title: AlphaGo Beats Lee Sedol
events.blurb: A London-based artificial intelligence laboratory's go-playing program, trained on millions of human games and then on games it had played against itself, defeated the reigning world champion of the ancient Asian board game 4–1 in a five-game match in Seoul. The match was broadcast live to 280 million people. Experts had predicted a champion-beating go program was a decade away; the algorithmic gap between games like chess and go had seemed insurmountable.
events.revealBlurb: March 15, 2016 — DeepMind's AlphaGo vs. Lee Sedol. Lee's single winning game, move 78 — the "divine move" — exploited a subtle blind spot in the AI. DeepMind was acquired by Google in 2014 for around $500 million. Lee retired from professional go three years later, partly because AI had changed the game.

events.title: Marie Curie Wins Nobel Prize
events.blurb: A 36-year-old Polish-born physicist working in a converted shed in a French capital became the first woman to win the world's most prestigious scientific prize, sharing a physics award with her husband and a French colleague for their research into radioactivity. She would win it a second time, alone, in chemistry eight years later. Her notebooks are still radioactive, stored in lead-lined boxes and read only in protective clothing.
events.revealBlurb: December 10, 1903 — shared with Pierre Curie and Henri Becquerel. She later became the first person, of any gender, to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences. Her daughter Irène won a Nobel in chemistry too.

events.title: Girl Scouts Founded
events.blurb: A 51-year-old widow in a Georgia city, inspired by a chance meeting with the British founder of a boys' scouting movement, gathered 18 girls in her house for a first troop meeting. She promised them learning to "do something with their lives, something the world would remember them for." Within a decade the organization had 70,000 members; within a century, over three million.
events.revealBlurb: March 12, 1912 — Juliette "Daisy" Gordon Low in Savannah. The signature cookies came 11 years later. Daisy had been deaf in one ear from wedding-day rice thrown into it; she joked about it lifelong.

events.title: The Feminine Mystique Published
events.blurb: A former labour journalist who had been writing articles for women's magazines published a 410-page book analyzing what she called "the problem that has no name" — the stifling dissatisfaction of educated suburban housewives. It sold three million copies within three years and became the foundational text of a resurgent American feminist movement that would transform employment law, education policy, and reproductive rights.
events.revealBlurb: February 19, 1963 — Betty Friedan. The book drew on her research into a Smith College alumni survey. Friedan went on to co-found the National Organization for Women in 1966 and help lead the 1970 Women's Strike for Equality.

events.title: Margaret Thatcher Becomes PM
events.blurb: The leader of the British Conservative Party, a grocer's daughter who had studied chemistry at Oxford and later trained as a barrister, was invited by the monarch to form a government after her party won a sweeping parliamentary majority. She became the United Kingdom's first woman prime minister and would hold the office for 11 years — the longest continuous premiership of the 20th century.
events.revealBlurb: May 4, 1979 — she took office quoting St. Francis of Assisi on the doorstep: "Where there is discord, may we bring harmony." The next decade would be anything but that. She was forced to resign by her own cabinet in November 1990.

events.title: Anita Hill Testifies
events.blurb: A 35-year-old law professor at a large university in the central U.S., subpoenaed by the Senate Judiciary Committee considering a Supreme Court nomination, testified publicly on live television that the nominee — her former supervisor at a federal agency — had sexually harassed her nearly a decade earlier. The all-male Senate committee confirmed him anyway by a 52-48 vote. The hearings galvanized a wave of women candidates; 47 won congressional seats the following year.
events.revealBlurb: October 11-13, 1991 — Hill testified against Clarence Thomas. Thomas was confirmed October 15 and is still on the Court. The 1992 elections were dubbed "the Year of the Woman" — though they still left women only 10 percent of Congress.

events.title: Marbury v. Madison: Judicial Review Established
events.blurb: Chief Justice John Marshall wrote the unanimous Supreme Court opinion in a case about a disputed judicial appointment, using it to announce that federal courts possessed the power to strike down laws they found incompatible with the Constitution — a power the Constitution itself does not explicitly mention. The ruling transformed the Supreme Court from the weakest branch of government into an equal arbiter of constitutional meaning.
events.revealBlurb: February 24, 1803 — Washington, D.C. Marshall's genius was ruling against Marbury (who wanted his commission) so Jefferson couldn't refuse to comply, while simultaneously claiming the Court's enormous new power. Jefferson privately hated the decision but was trapped. The ruling wasn't used to strike down another law for 54 more years.

events.title: Haymarket Bombing, Chicago
events.blurb: At a labor rally in Chicago's Haymarket Square called to protest the police killing of striking workers the previous day, an unknown person threw a dynamite bomb into a column of police officers, killing seven officers and at least four civilians in the ensuing explosion and gunfire. The incident became the defining trauma of American labor radicalism and led to the hanging of four men for conspiracy, despite the bomber's identity never being established.
events.revealBlurb: May 4, 1886 — Haymarket Square, Chicago. Nobody has ever been identified as the bomber. Governor John Altgeld pardoned the surviving defendants in 1893, calling the trial a miscarriage of justice — and was destroyed politically for it. The date May 4 became International Workers' Day in much of the world as a result of the Haymarket executions.

events.title: Bush v. Gore Halts Florida Recount
events.blurb: The Supreme Court ruled 5–4 to halt the manual recount of Florida's contested presidential ballots, effectively awarding the state's 25 electoral votes to Republican George W. Bush and deciding the closest presidential election since 1876. The margin in Florida's certified count was 537 votes out of nearly 6 million cast; Al Gore ultimately conceded, and Bush won the presidency 271–266 in the Electoral College.
events.revealBlurb: December 12, 2000 — Washington, D.C. The per curiam opinion included the extraordinary disclaimer that the ruling "is limited to the present circumstances" and should not be treated as precedent. The butterfly ballot design in Palm Beach County alone may have cost Gore 2,000–3,000 votes to Pat Buchanan.

events.title: September 11 Terrorist Attacks
events.blurb: That morning, 19 al-Qaeda hijackers commandeered four commercial aircraft and flew two into the Twin Towers of the World Trade Center, one into the Pentagon, and a fourth — whose passengers revolted and forced the plane down — into a field near Shanksville, Pennsylvania. The attacks killed 2,977 people and triggered the United States' longest wars, a sweeping reorganization of domestic security, and a generation of political consequence.
events.revealBlurb: September 11, 2001 — New York, Virginia, Pennsylvania. The North Tower stood 102 minutes after impact; the South Tower collapsed first, 56 minutes after being hit, because the plane struck lower floors. The 9/11 Commission found no credible evidence of state sponsorship by any foreign government.

events.title: U.S. Invades Iraq
events.blurb: A U.S.-led coalition launched air strikes and a ground invasion of Iraq in a "shock and awe" campaign code-named Operation Iraqi Freedom, premised on intelligence assessments — later found to be wrong — that Saddam Hussein possessed weapons of mass destruction. The initial combat phase lasted 41 days; the subsequent occupation and insurgency lasted until 2011 and killed more than 4,400 American service members.
events.revealBlurb: March 20, 2003 — Baghdad, Iraq. No weapons of mass destruction were found. Saddam Hussein was captured hiding in a hole near Tikrit in December 2003 and executed by hanging in December 2006. President Bush declared "Mission Accomplished" on May 1, 2003, from the deck of an aircraft carrier; the war continued for eight more years.

events.title: Julius and Ethel Rosenberg Executed
events.blurb: Julius and Ethel Rosenberg were executed by electric chair at Sing Sing Prison, having been convicted of passing atomic bomb design secrets to the Soviet Union — making them the only American civilians executed for espionage during the Cold War. Their case divided the nation, with their guilt debated in editorial pages, union halls, and diplomatic cables around the world.
events.revealBlurb: June 19, 1953 — Ossining, New York. Ethel Rosenberg required three jolts of electricity before she died; Julius was pronounced dead after the first. Subsequent release of Soviet archives confirmed Julius was a spy; historians still debate the extent of Ethel's involvement.

events.title: Khrushchev Secret Speech
events.blurb: Speaking to a closed session of the Soviet Communist Party's 20th Congress, a new premier delivered a four-hour denunciation of his predecessor's personality cult, show trials, and mass purges. The text was supposed to remain secret but leaked within months, shattering communist movements worldwide and launching a partial cultural thaw at home.
events.revealBlurb: February 25, 1956 — Nikita Khrushchev, three years after Stalin's death. A Polish journalist smuggled the text to Israeli intelligence, who gave it to the CIA. Millions of Soviet prisoners were rehabilitated in the following years.

events.title: Cuban Missile Crisis Address
events.blurb: An American president delivered a 17-minute televised address revealing that Soviet nuclear missiles had been discovered on a Caribbean island 145 kilometres from Florida, demanding their removal within a strict deadline. The 13-day standoff that followed was the closest the Cold War came to nuclear exchange, with submarines on both sides carrying armed torpedoes.

events.title: Nixon Visits China
events.blurb: A U.S. president whose entire career had been built on anti-communist credentials stepped off Air Force One in the Chinese capital to shake hands with the leader of a nation Washington had refused to recognize for 23 years. The week-long visit, carefully choreographed after two years of secret diplomacy, upended the bipolar world order and drove a wedge between the two great communist powers.
events.revealBlurb: February 21-28, 1972 — Richard Nixon meets Mao Zedong. Henry Kissinger had flown secretly to Beijing via Pakistan the previous summer to arrange it. The phrase "Nixon goes to China" has since become shorthand for a politician doing something only his base could forgive.

events.title: SALT I Signed
events.blurb: In the ornate Vladimir Hall of the Kremlin, the leaders of the two superpowers signed the first treaty limiting strategic nuclear weapons. It froze the number of intercontinental and submarine-launched ballistic missiles on each side at then-current levels and restricted anti-missile defenses. Neither arsenal shrank, but the race for ever more warheads finally acquired guardrails.
events.revealBlurb: May 26, 1972 — Nixon and Brezhnev in Moscow. The ABM Treaty signed the same day restricted each side to two (later one) missile defense sites. The US withdrew from it in 2002 under George W. Bush.

events.title: First World Series
events.blurb: A best-of-nine championship series between the American League and National League pennant winners was played — the first time the two major leagues had agreed to a postseason championship after years of cold war. An underdog American League team, the Boston Americans, defeated the heavily favoured Pittsburgh Pirates 5 games to 3. The Pirates' owner, Barney Dreyfuss, had proposed the series himself.
events.revealBlurb: October 1-13, 1903 — Boston Americans (later the Red Sox) beat the Pittsburgh Pirates. Cy Young, Boston's 36-year-old ace, started game 3 but was the losing pitcher. Dreyfuss gave his losing Pirates a share of the winners' purse to compensate. No World Series was held in 1904; it became annual from 1905.

events.title: Secretariat Wins Triple Crown
events.blurb: A 3-year-old chestnut colt won the third leg of the American Triple Crown — a 2,414-metre New York race that had defeated the previous eight Kentucky Derby and Preakness winners — by 31 lengths in a time so fast it broke the dirt-track world record by 2.4 seconds. His time has never been approached. He ran the final quarter mile faster than his first, an impossibility for thoroughbreds under hard exertion. His heart, when examined at autopsy, was more than double the size of a normal horse's.
events.revealBlurb: June 9, 1973 — Secretariat at Belmont Park. Jockey Ron Turcotte. The closest horse at the finish was 31 lengths behind — literally out of the camera frame in live television shots. Secretariat retired to stud later that year; his daughters and granddaughters have dominated American thoroughbred breeding for decades.
