events.title: Miracle on Ice
events.blurb: A U.S. college-aged men's hockey team, facing a Soviet Union team that had won five of the previous six Olympic gold medals and was widely considered the best in the world, won 4-3 at a Lake Placid Winter Olympics with a third-period game-winning goal by the team's captain. The victory, during a tense period of Cold War tensions and a national recession, was broadcast on delayed tape; the announcer's closing cry — "Do you believe in miracles? YES!" — became one of the most-replayed lines in American sports.
events.revealBlurb: February 22, 1980 — US vs USSR at the Lake Placid Olympics. Coach: Herb Brooks. The US went on to win the gold medal by beating Finland two days later. The captain was Mike Eruzione. Al Michaels was the ABC announcer.

events.title: Phelps Wins 8 Golds in Beijing
events.blurb: A 23-year-old American swimmer won his eighth gold medal of a single Summer Olympic Games — surpassing Mark Spitz's 36-year-old record for most golds in a single Olympics. He set or broke world records in seven of the events. His final gold came in the 4x100m medley relay. Over four Olympic Games he would win a career total of 23 golds and 28 total medals, more than any athlete in any sport before him.
events.revealBlurb: August 17, 2008 — Michael Phelps at the Beijing Olympics. Spitz's previous record was 7 golds from 1972 Munich. Phelps's career gold total eventually reached 23; he retired after Rio 2016. Spitz had been a rumored spectator at many of Phelps's events.

events.title: Messi Wins World Cup
events.blurb: A 35-year-old Argentine forward, in his fifth and final World Cup tournament, led his team to a 3-3 draw against France in the final, then won a penalty shootout 4-2 at a Qatari stadium. He scored two of the final's goals himself, then converted his penalty. The tournament's signature absence from his glittering career — the World Cup — was at last his. It was widely described as the greatest World Cup final ever played.
events.revealBlurb: December 18, 2022 — Argentina 3-3 France (4-2 pens), Lusail Stadium, Qatar. Messi and Kylian Mbappé combined for six goals between them. Messi had already won seven Ballon d'Or awards, a record; he would win an eighth in 2023. Mbappé became the first to score a hat-trick in a World Cup final since Geoff Hurst in 1966.

events.title: Scuttling of the Graf Spee
events.blurb: A feared commerce-raider that had sunk nine merchant ships in three months limped into a neutral harbour for repairs after a running battle with three smaller cruisers, then sat immobile while international diplomacy set a 72-hour countdown. Twenty thousand spectators lined the waterfront to watch her captain make his final decision.
events.revealBlurb: December 17, 1939, Montevideo. Captain Hans Langsdorff scuttled the Admiral Graf Spee at 8:55 PM rather than risk his crew in what he believed was an overwhelming British trap. Three days later he wrapped himself in the ship's battle ensign and shot himself. The trap was largely bluff.

events.title: Fall of France
events.blurb: German armoured divisions crossed a forested highland deemed impassable by military doctrine, bypassed the most elaborate fixed defences in Europe, and in six weeks forced the capitulation of a nation whose army was considered the strongest on the continent. An armistice was signed in the same railway carriage used for the previous war's peace.
events.revealBlurb: May 10 – June 22, 1940. The armistice was signed at Compiègne in Hitler's deliberate reversal of the 1918 Armistice humiliation — he had the original railway carriage brought out of a museum. France lost 92,000 killed in six weeks. A junior general named de Gaulle flew to London and refused to accept the result.

events.title: Lend-Lease Act Signed
events.blurb: A nation officially at peace passed legislation allowing its president to lend, lease, or otherwise transfer war materials to any country whose defence he deemed vital to national security, bypassing a strict neutrality law without technically entering the conflict. The first shipments moved within weeks, directed at an island nation running critically short of everything.
events.revealBlurb: March 11, 1941 — FDR signed H.R. 1776 (the bill number was a deliberate wink). By the end of the programme, the US had shipped $50 billion in supplies — equivalent to roughly $800 billion today — to 38 countries. The Soviet Union received about 17 million tons of equipment, including 400,000 jeeps and trucks.

events.title: Battle of the Coral Sea
events.blurb: Two opposing fleets manoeuvred for days without either side's surface ships ever sighting the other, their aircraft flying hundreds of miles over open ocean to find and strike carriers whose decks they could not see. One navy lost a fleet carrier and the other lost a light carrier — but the strategic consequence was that an invasion convoy turned back.
events.revealBlurb: May 4–8, 1942 — the first naval battle in history fought entirely by aircraft. Neither fleet's ships came within sight of the other. Japan lost the light carrier Shōhō; the US lost USS Lexington. The two Japanese fleet carriers damaged at Coral Sea were then unavailable at Midway — a fact that proved decisive a month later.

events.title: Flag Raising on Iwo Jima
events.blurb: A photograph taken on a volcanic island's highest point captured six men raising a large flag over rubble and smoke, becoming one of the most reproduced images in history — and the model for a national memorial — though the battle it symbolised had barely begun and would last another five weeks at a cost exceeding 26,000 American casualties.
events.revealBlurb: February 23, 1945 — Joe Rosenthal's photograph was actually of the second flag raised that day; a smaller flag had gone up hours earlier. Three of the six men in the photograph were killed before the island was secured. Admiral Chester Nimitz observed: "Among the Americans who served on Iwo Jima, uncommon valor was a common virtue."

events.title: Alexander the Great Dies
events.blurb: A 32-year-old conqueror, having created an empire stretching from Macedonia to northwestern India in ten years of campaigning, died of fever (or poisoning — sources disagree) in a palace in a Mesopotamian capital while planning the next campaign, this one against Arabia. He left no clear heir; his generals divided the empire into warring successor states — the Hellenistic kingdoms — that shaped Mediterranean culture for the next three centuries.
events.revealBlurb: June 10 or 11, 323 BCE — Alexander III in Babylon. Asked on his deathbed to whom his empire should go, he reportedly said: "To the strongest." Competing theories for his death: malaria, typhoid, alcoholism, West Nile virus, poisoning by his general Antipater. His body was hijacked en route home by Ptolemy to Alexandria.

events.title: First Punic War Begins
events.blurb: The Roman Republic and the Carthaginian Empire, the two rising powers of the western Mediterranean, went to war over control of a large island between them. The conflict would last 23 years and transform Rome from a purely land-based power into a naval one — the Romans, ignorant of shipbuilding, reportedly reverse-engineered a captured Carthaginian warship to build their first fleet. Rome eventually won and imposed a crushing indemnity; the seed of two more wars was planted.
events.revealBlurb: 264 BCE — Rome vs. Carthage over Sicily. "Punic" comes from the Latin for "Phoenician," Carthage's origin. The Romans invented boarding bridges ("corvi") that turned sea battles into quasi-land battles they could win. Rome lost 700 ships over the course of the war, mostly to storms.

events.title: Han Dynasty Founded
events.blurb: A former peasant who had risen through the collapsing Qin military to become a rebel general defeated his principal rival in a civil war and declared himself emperor, founding a dynasty that would rule China for four centuries. The Han synthesized Confucian political theory with Qin administrative machinery, ran the Silk Road trade with the West, invented paper, cast iron plowshares, and effectively defined the imperial Chinese civilization that would persist until 1911. The ethnic majority of modern China still calls itself "Han."
events.revealBlurb: 202 BCE — Liu Bang, posthumously Emperor Gaozu. He defeated Xiang Yu at the Battle of Gaixia. The Han dynasty is conventionally divided into the Western Han (202 BCE - 9 CE) and Eastern Han (25 CE - 220 CE), with a brief Wang Mang interregnum between.

events.title: Augustus Becomes Emperor
events.blurb: The Roman Senate formally voted a new series of titles and powers to the victor of the civil wars that had ended the Republic — including "Augustus" (the revered), "Princeps" (first citizen), and various senatorial and tribunicial powers. The Republic's forms were maintained — the Senate met, consuls were elected — but real power now flowed through the man at the top. The Roman Empire had begun. Its first emperor would reign 41 years and die of natural causes in his 75th year.
events.revealBlurb: January 16, 27 BCE — Octavian accepts the title "Augustus." He preferred the title "Princeps"; only later emperors would unambiguously style themselves "Imperator." The month August is named for him. He outlived his designated heirs repeatedly; his step-son Tiberius eventually succeeded him in 14 CE.

events.title: The Antonine Plague
events.blurb: Soldiers returning from campaigns in Parthia brought a disease — almost certainly smallpox — that spread from the eastern frontier through every province of the empire over fifteen years. The physician Galen, the most famous doctor of his age, documented symptoms in detail from Rome itself; at the plague's peak witnesses recorded 2,000 deaths per day in the capital alone.
events.revealBlurb: 165–180 CE. Galen's treatment recommendation included keeping patients warm and feeding them milk — the best care available, and completely ineffective. The plague killed co-emperor Lucius Verus in 169 CE and may have killed up to 10% of the empire's total population.

events.title: Handel's Messiah Premieres
events.blurb: A 57-year-old German-born, London-resident composer conducted the premiere of a three-hour oratorio he had written in 24 days, at a charity concert in a hall in an Irish capital. Ladies were asked not to wear hoops and gentlemen not to wear swords so more could fit in the venue. The proceeds benefited a hospital, a prison society, and a charitable infirmary. Two of the inmates were released on the night using the concert's proceeds.
events.revealBlurb: April 13, 1742 — George Frideric Handel at the Great Music Hall on Fishamble Street, Dublin. The "Hallelujah Chorus" became a standing-ovation custom. It's rumored King George II stood at its London premiere; no contemporary source confirms the story.

events.title: Beethoven's Ninth Premieres
events.blurb: A nearly deaf 53-year-old composer, standing on the podium while a co-conductor did the actual directing, premiered a vast hour-long symphony that broke with convention by adding four vocal soloists and a chorus to the orchestra in its final movement. The text was a Schiller poem celebrating universal brotherhood. At the end the composer had to be turned around by one of the singers to see the audience — which he otherwise could not hear — thundering applause.
events.revealBlurb: May 7, 1824 — Ludwig van Beethoven at the Theater am Kärntnertor, Vienna. He had been profoundly deaf for over a decade. The "Ode to Joy" theme is now, somewhat jarringly given the text, the official anthem of the European Union.

events.title: Wagner's Ring Cycle Premieres
events.blurb: A 63-year-old German composer presented the first complete four-night performance of a 15-hour operatic cycle he had been writing, off and on, for 26 years, at a festival opera house in a Bavarian town he had specifically had built to host it. Audiences included Tchaikovsky, Liszt, Grieg, Bruckner, the emperor of Germany, and the emperor of Brazil. The complete run was a financial disaster.
events.revealBlurb: August 13-17, 1876 — Richard Wagner at the Bayreuth Festspielhaus, Bayreuth. The festival runs to this day; tickets are difficult to obtain. Wagner's anti-Semitic essays, and the Nazi regime's later embrace of his work, have cast a lasting shadow.

events.title: Tchaikovsky's Swan Lake Premieres
events.blurb: A 36-year-old Russian composer's first full-length ballet score premiered at a grand theatre in the Russian capital, paired with choreography that was widely thought incompetent and dancing that was widely thought under-rehearsed. Critics focused their complaints on the music, which they found too "symphonic" for dancing. Only after the composer's death, in a restaged 1895 version with new choreography, did the ballet become a classic.
events.revealBlurb: March 4, 1877 — Pyotr Tchaikovsky's Swan Lake at the Bolshoi, Moscow (Old Style February 20). The 1895 St. Petersburg revival with Petipa/Ivanov choreography is the version most companies perform today. The tragic black-swan finale was a 1950s restoration.

events.title: First Jazz Recording
events.blurb: Five white musicians from New Orleans, working under the slightly misspelled name "Original Dixieland Jass Band," recorded two sides for a Victor label at a New York studio: "Livery Stable Blues" and "Dixie Jass Band One Step." The 78 sold a million copies, breaking sales records, and introduced the word "jazz" to most Americans. Black New Orleans musicians had been playing the style for years; the first commercial recording went to imitators.
events.revealBlurb: February 26, 1917 — recorded in NYC; released March 7, 1917. The ODJB's cornetist Nick LaRocca later claimed, implausibly, to have invented jazz. The ethical irony of white performers first commercializing a Black art form was noted at the time and has only grown.

events.title: Madonna's "Like a Prayer" Video
events.blurb: The music video for a 30-year-old singer's new single, featuring burning crosses, stigmata, and the singer kissing a Black saint statue coming to life, premiered during a Pepsi commercial at the start of a television special paid for by the soft-drink company. The Vatican condemned the video as blasphemous; conservative Christian groups organized boycotts; Pepsi paid the singer $5 million to sever their sponsorship deal. Her album sold 15 million copies.
events.revealBlurb: March 2, 1989 — the Pepsi commercial; the full video premiered on MTV March 3. Director Mary Lambert. The controversy gave Madonna an estimated $5 million for the Pepsi deal plus enormous free publicity; she kept the money. The album "Like a Prayer" remains her best-reviewed.

events.title: The Simpsons Premieres
events.blurb: A half-hour animated primetime sitcom about a dysfunctional yellow-skinned family in the fictional American town of Springfield premiered as a Christmas special on a fledgling US television network. The show's acerbic satire, cartoon slapstick, and unprecedented crossover appeal — with children and adults watching together — established animation as a legitimate prime-time format. It is still in production three and a half decades later, the longest-running American scripted prime-time TV series.
events.revealBlurb: December 17, 1989 — the Christmas special "Simpsons Roasting on an Open Fire" on the Fox network. Created by Matt Groening from shorts he had been making for The Tracey Ullman Show since 1987. The family was named after Groening's own family except Bart, an anagram of "brat."

events.title: Spice Girls' "Wannabe"
events.blurb: A British pop group of five young women released their debut single — a bouncy three-minute track with a rap-like opening, shot on a single take in a Lisbon hotel — hit number one in 37 countries over the following months. The five — styled "Scary," "Sporty," "Baby," "Ginger," and "Posh" — would dominate late-1990s pop culture with a "Girl Power" message that was earnest, commercial, and enormously successful. They sold 100 million records globally.
events.revealBlurb: July 8, 1996 — Spice Girls: Melanie B (Scary), Melanie C (Sporty), Emma Bunton (Baby), Geri Halliwell (Ginger), Victoria Adams (Posh). The video was shot in a single day at the Hotel Palácio in Portugal. Victoria Beckham married David Beckham in 1999; she launched a fashion career later.

events.title: Titanic Released
events.blurb: A Canadian director released a 195-minute romantic epic about a fictional couple aboard the 1912 maiden voyage of the British ocean liner. The production had been the most expensive in Hollywood history, its budget having doubled during filming; industry wags predicted financial disaster. The film ran in theatres for ten months, won 11 Oscars, and became the first film to gross over a billion dollars. Its director famously shouted "I'm king of the world" from the podium.
events.revealBlurb: December 19, 1997 — James Cameron, starring Leonardo DiCaprio and Kate Winslet. It grossed $2.2 billion; Cameron's subsequent "Avatar" beat it 12 years later, also directed by him. Celine Dion's "My Heart Will Go On" spent three weeks at #1.

events.title: Furby Released
events.blurb: A battery-operated toy furry pet that could speak, move its eyes, and apparently learn English words from "Furbish" over time became the must-have Christmas gift of the season. Parents who had lived through the Cabbage Patch Kids and Tickle Me Elmo crazes of previous years went through it again. The National Security Agency banned them from their premises, reportedly out of concern that they might record classified conversations and "repeat" them.
events.revealBlurb: October 2, 1998 — Tiger Electronics. 40 million Furbys sold in the first three years. The NSA's ban was based on a misunderstanding of the toy's technology — it had no recording capability at all; "learning" was a pre-programmed script that made the toy seem to become more English-speaking over time.

events.title: Nintendo Famicom Launches in Japan
events.blurb: A cheap red-and-white 8-bit console hit Japanese shelves the same day as a competing machine. Within a year it had outsold every rival combined, driven fourteen manufacturers out of the market entirely, and established Nintendo as the unchallenged ruler of the Japanese gaming business.
events.revealBlurb: July 15, 1983 — Nintendo's Family Computer launched in Japan at ¥14,800, head-to-head with Sega's SG-1000. The NES version launched in New York in October 1985. The NES/Famicom line sold 61.91 million units worldwide.

events.title: Pokémon Red and Green Released in Japan
events.blurb: A game about capturing and training pocket monsters on a handheld with a dying link cable had been in development for six years and nearly bankrupted its studio twice. It released quietly on a console most retailers considered obsolete. Within months it had detonated into the fastest-growing entertainment franchise in Japanese history.
events.revealBlurb: February 27, 1996 — Pokémon Red and Green launched for Game Boy in Japan. By the end of 1996 they had sold 3.6 million copies in Japan alone; the franchise has since generated over $150 billion, making it the highest-grossing media franchise in history.

events.title: Counter-Strike Released as Standalone
events.blurb: Two amateur developers built a modification for Half-Life in which terrorists and counter-terrorists fought in small tactical maps. Valve noticed the mod's download numbers, purchased the rights, and released it as a standalone product. It became the most-played online game in the world for over a decade, the game credited with institutionalising competitive PC gaming.
events.revealBlurb: November 9, 2000 — Counter-Strike version 1.0 released as a free Half-Life modification. Creators Minh "Gooseman" Le and Jess Cliffe had started the mod in June 1999. In 2023, CS:GO/CS2 peaked at over 1.8 million concurrent Steam players.

events.title: Oculus Rift Kickstarter Campaign Launches
events.blurb: A 19-year-old in his parents' garage had spent years building virtual reality headsets from scavenged parts. His Kickstarter campaign asked for $250,000 to build a developer kit. It raised $2.4 million from nearly 10,000 backers. Two years later, Facebook acquired his company for $2 billion.
events.revealBlurb: August 1, 2012 — Palmer Luckey launched the Oculus Rift Kickstarter, raising 974% of its $250,000 goal. Facebook (now Meta) acquired Oculus VR in March 2014 for approximately $2 billion.

events.title: Red Dead Redemption 2 Released
events.blurb: A cowboy open-world game with a 60-hour main story, simulated beard growth, morality consequences for every interaction, and a horse whose bond with the player affected its responsiveness opened the largest weekend in entertainment history. It earned $725 million in three days.
events.revealBlurb: October 26, 2018 — Red Dead Redemption 2 launched for PlayStation 4 and Xbox One. It shipped 17 million copies in its first thirteen days. The game has now sold over 79 million copies. Development reportedly involved teams working 100-hour weeks across five years.

events.title: Galveston Hurricane
events.blurb: A Category 4 storm made landfall at a Gulf Coast barrier-island city, then the wealthiest in Texas, with a 4.6-metre storm surge that overtopped the highest point of the island. Roughly 8,000 people — nearly a quarter of the population — were killed in a single night. It remains the deadliest natural disaster in U.S. history.
events.revealBlurb: September 8, 1900 — Galveston, Texas. After the storm, the city built a 5-metre seawall and physically raised the entire island by up to 5 metres using sand pumped from the harbor. Houston, inland and safer, permanently overtook Galveston as the state's economic center.

events.title: Triangle Shirtwaist Factory Fire
events.blurb: A fire that broke out in a garment factory occupying the top three floors of a ten-story building in Manhattan's Greenwich Village killed 146 workers — mostly young immigrant women — in less than 18 minutes. Many died because exit doors had been locked from the outside; dozens jumped from the eighth, ninth, and tenth floors to their deaths on the sidewalk below, in full view of horrified onlookers.
events.revealBlurb: March 25, 1911 — Washington Place, New York City. The factory owners were indicted for manslaughter and acquitted, then collected on inflated insurance claims. The disaster triggered passage of more than 30 new labor safety laws in New York State.

events.title: Spanish Flu Pandemic Begins
events.blurb: An unusually lethal strain of influenza, carried through military camps and troop ships during the final months of a world war, infected a third of the planet and killed an estimated 50 to 100 million people in three successive waves over two years. Unlike most flus, it disproportionately killed healthy young adults by triggering cytokine storms in robust immune systems.
events.revealBlurb: March 1918 — first identified at a US Army base in Kansas. It was called "Spanish" only because wartime censorship in belligerent countries suppressed coverage; neutral Spain reported it freely, so it seemed to originate there. It had nothing to do with Spain.

events.title: Hurricane Katrina
events.blurb: A Category 3 hurricane made landfall on the US Gulf Coast, driving a storm surge that overtopped and breached the levee system protecting a major port city lying largely below sea level. 80 percent of the city flooded; 1,392 people died. The chaotic federal response — images of thousands stranded on a sports stadium roof, bodies floating in water — inflicted lasting damage on the administration in power.
events.revealBlurb: August 29, 2005 — New Orleans, Louisiana. The Superdome housed 30,000 evacuees for five days in deteriorating conditions. The head of FEMA, Michael Brown, had previously run the International Arabian Horse Association; he resigned within two weeks.

events.title: Typhoon Haiyan
events.blurb: One of the strongest tropical cyclones ever recorded at landfall — with sustained winds of 315 km/h — struck the central Philippines, obliterating coastal cities. A 7-metre storm surge drove ships onto city streets; the city of Tacloban lost most of its infrastructure. At least 6,300 people died, and 4 million were displaced.
events.revealBlurb: November 8, 2013 — Leyte province. The Filipino lead negotiator at the UN climate talks that week gave a tearful speech and began a hunger strike until "meaningful progress" was made. His country's delegation wore black.
